**GitHub repo:** <https://github.com/yourusername/ec422_ps3_cachoua>

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)

retail_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/retail_sales_raw.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    RSAFS = col_double(),
    RSAFSNA = col_double()
  )
)
```

## Time and Tsibbles

**The data.** `retail_ts` holds two series from the U.S. Census Bureau's monthly retail trade survey, downloaded manually from FRED: **RSAFS** (Advance Retail Sales: Retail Trade and Food Services, seasonally adjusted) and **RSAFSNA** (the same series, not seasonally adjusted), both in millions of dollars, monthly, January 1992 – September 2026. It is stored in long format with **index** `Month` (a `yearmonth`) and **key** `series_id`. `can_gas` comes from the `canadian_gas` tsibble in `fpp3`: monthly Canadian natural gas production in billions of cubic meters, January 1960 – February 2005. Its **index** is `Month`, and it has **no key** because it holds a single series.

### Reading dates (2.2)

```{r}
head(read_csv("data/retail_sales_raw.csv", show_col_types = FALSE))
```

**2.2a.** `read_csv()` guessed correctly: `observation_date` is read as `<date>` because FRED uses ISO-8601 dates (YYYY-MM-DD). We still re-read the file with an explicit `col_types` specification (setup chunk above) and `na = "."` so FRED's missing-value marker is handled.

### Long format and the tsibble (2.3–2.4)

```{r}
retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>
  select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA), names_to = "series_id", values_to = "sales")

head(retail_raw_long)

retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)

head(retail_ts)
has_gaps(retail_ts)
```

The header reads `[1M]`, so the tsibble correctly detected a monthly frequency, and `has_gaps()` returns `FALSE` for both series, so there are no missing months.

### Canadian gas (2.5)

```{r}
key_vars(canadian_gas)
index_var(canadian_gas)

can_gas <- canadian_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume)

has_gaps(can_gas)
head(can_gas)
```

### Working with dates (2.6)

```{r}
can_gas_recent <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan")) |>
  mutate(year    = year(Month),
         month   = month(Month, label = TRUE),
         quarter = quarter(Month))

can_gas_recent |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(avg_volume = mean(Volume)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Month", "Average volume (bcm)"))
```

**2.6b.** Since 1990, **December** has the highest average production (≈17.1 bcm, with January close behind at ≈17.0), and **June** has the lowest (≈14.9 bcm).

```{r}
can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(next_month           = Month + 1,
         same_month_last_year = Month - 12) |>
  head()
```

**2.6c.** On a `yearmonth` index, `+ 1` moves forward one month and `- 12` moves back one year. On an ordinary `Date` like `observation_date`, `+ 1` would move forward one day (e.g. 1992-01-01 → 1992-01-02).

```{r}
can_gas_q <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>
  index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>
  summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))

head(can_gas_q)
can_gas_q |> autoplot(Volume) + theme_minimal()
```

**2.6d.** Gas production is a *flow*: each monthly value is the amount produced during that month, so quarterly production is the total of the three months. A mean would give average monthly production in the quarter, not quarterly production. The quarterly series is still clearly seasonal, with a repeating sawtooth pattern: Q1 and Q4 (winter) are high and Q2–Q3 are low.

### Plotting with autoplot() (2.7)

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**2.7b.** The NSA series has a strong pattern that repeats each year: a large spike every December (holiday shopping), followed by a sharp drop in January–February, with smaller bumps in spring and summer. The SA series doesn't have this sawtooth pattern. It runs smoothly through the middle of the NSA swings. Over the long run, the two series follow the same path. Both show the same upward trend, the same 2008–09 recession decline, the sharp COVID collapse in spring 2020, and the strong 2021 rebound. Seasonal adjustment removes only the within-year calendar pattern. It doesn't change the trend or the business-cycle movements.

```{r}
can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    subtitle = "Monthly, January 1960 – February 2005",
    x = NULL, y = "Billions of cubic meters"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "B")) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales with LOESS Trend",
    x = NULL, y = "Sales (billions of dollars)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**2.7d.** I added a dashed `geom_smooth()` LOESS trend line to show the long-run path without the month-to-month noise. I also used `scale_y_continuous()` to relabel the axis in billions of dollars (e.g. "$400B"), which is easier to read than scientific notation like `4e+05`.

## Transformations

### Logs (3.1)

**3.1a.** The seasonal swings in `can_gas` do grow with the level, but not over the whole sample. They are small in the 1960s, grow steadily through the 1970s, and are largest in the late 1970s–1980s, when production had levelled off around 8–10 bcm. From about 1990 onward, production keeps rising toward 15–19 bcm, but the swings shrink rather than grow. So the size of the seasonal pattern changes over time in a way that isn't just proportional to the level.

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))

can_gas |>
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Log of Canadian Gas Production", x = NULL, y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.1b.** After taking logs, the very steep early growth (1960s) is compressed and the trend looks concave: rapid growth early, then flattening. The seasonal swings in the 1960s now look about as large as those in the 1980s, while the post-1990 swings look even smaller than before. Logs are a reasonable choice for `can_gas` because production grows roughly exponentially early on, and the swings scale with the level for the first few decades. They don't fix everything, though. Even on the log scale, the seasonal amplitude shrinks a lot after 1990, so no single constant seasonal pattern fits the whole sample. I'd still use logs (they make growth rates easy to read and stabilize the early period), but I'd keep in mind that the seasonality is changing over time.

```{r}
retail_nsa <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales))

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "NSA Retail Sales (Level)", x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(title = "NSA Retail Sales (Log)", x = NULL, y = "log(sales)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.1c.** The case for logging NSA retail sales is stronger than for `can_gas`. In levels, the December spikes and January drops grow steadily as sales rise (a classic multiplicative pattern), and on the log scale the seasonal swings are roughly constant in size and the trend is close to a straight line.

### Growth rates (3.2)

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_direct = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume),
    growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff)
  )

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas Production: Month-over-Month Growth",
       x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(title = "Gap Between Exact and Log-Difference Growth Rates",
       x = NULL, y = "Absolute difference (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()

summary(can_gas$growth_gap)
```

**3.2a.** The log-difference approximation is very good here. The median gap is about 0.14 percentage points, and gaps above 1–2 points only occur in the few months with very large growth rates (±15–25%, mostly in the 1960s–70s), which is when the approximation is known to get worse.

### SA vs. NSA growth (3.3)

```{r}
retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(series_id) |>
  summarize(sd_growth = sd(growth_mom, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Series", "SD of m/m growth (%)"))
```

**3.3.** The NSA growth rate is far noisier: its standard deviation is about 9.6 percentage points versus about 1.7 for SA. NSA growth swings to roughly +15–20% every December and −20 to −25% every January because of the holiday cycle seen in 2.7b. The SA growth rate hovers near zero, and its only large moves are real economic events (the 2008 recession, the COVID drop and rebound in 2020). Most of the month-to-month variation in the NSA series is predictable seasonality, not news about the economy.

## Seasonality

### Season plots (4.1)

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales", y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales", y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.1b.** In the NSA season plot, every year traces the same shape: low in January–February, a jump in March, a bump in May, a dip in September, and a large peak in December. In the SA season plot, each year's line is essentially flat, rising slightly within the year because of trend growth. The only visible within-year shape is the April 2020 COVID drop, which is a real event, not seasonality. Seasonal adjustment removes the repeating calendar shape and leaves trend, cycle and irregular movements.

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in Canadian Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.1c.** Gas production is highest in the winter months (December–January, with February–March also high) and lowest in summer (June–September). That fits intuition: natural gas is mainly used for heating in Canada (and in the U.S., which imports Canadian gas), so demand peaks in winter. The plot also shows that the summer dip is deep in the early years and much shallower in the most recent years.

### Subseries plot (4.2)

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)")
```

The blue monthly means are highest for December and January and lowest for June–September, which confirms the winter-peak pattern. Every month shares the same rising, flattening trend.

### X-13ARIMA-SEATS (4.3)

```{r}
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()

retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()

retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(month = month(Month, label = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(avg = mean(seasonal), min = min(seasonal), max = max(seasonal)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "X-13 seasonal factors by calendar month")
```

**4.3a.** The seasonal factor is highest in **December**, averaging about 1.15, so December sales are typically about 15% above trend (February is lowest at about 0.89, roughly 11% below trend). The swings shrink over time. The December factor falls from about 1.21 in 1992 to about 1.16 in the 2000s and about 1.10 by 2019–2025, probably because holiday spending has spread into November and online shopping has smoothed the calendar pattern.

```{r}
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
       x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

summary(sa_compare$pct_diff)
```

**4.3b.** My default X-13 adjustment matches the official series closely. The difference is centered on zero, half of all months are within about ±0.15%, and the largest gap is under 2%. The biggest differences come after 2019, especially in January (2021–2024 are 1.4–1.8% above the Census figure) and around the COVID period. That is where the Census Bureau's custom treatment of outliers, holidays and trading days, and its separate adjustment of each retail category, matters most.

### Linear trend + seasonal dummies (4.4)

```{r}
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))

can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

**4.4a.** The trend coefficient is about 0.00397, so production grew on average about **0.40% per month** (roughly 4.9% per year). All seasonal coefficients are relative to January. The month with the most significant seasonal effect is **June** (`season()year6`), with an estimate of −0.251 (about 25 log points below January) and t ≈ −4.78. July, August and September are also strongly negative, while December is about equal to January (t ≈ 0.14).

```{r}
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.4b.** The fitted line gets the overall upward direction and the timing of the seasonal pattern right, but it misses the shape of the trend badly. The actual series is curved: it grows faster than the fitted line in the 1960s, sits well above it through the 1970s, falls below it in the 1980s plateau, and is above it again in the late 1990s before flattening below it after 2000. The fitted seasonal swings are also the same size every year, so they are too small early in the sample and too large after 1990.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**4.4c.** The residuals are clearly not white noise. The time plot shows long, slow waves (negative in the early 1960s, strongly positive in the 1970s, near zero or negative later), and the ACF decays very slowly and stays far outside the significance bands at every lag up to 24. The histogram is skewed, with a long left tail. The Ljung–Box statistic is about 7,774 with a p-value of essentially 0, so we strongly reject the null of no autocorrelation at the 5% level. Much of the structure left over could still be modeled.

## Forecast Evaluation

### Expanding window (5.1)

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Expanding-window TS-CV, 1-step-ahead")
```

**5.1a.** The first training sample is January 1960 – December 1979 (240 months), so the **first evaluated forecast is for January 1980**. The **last evaluated forecast is for February 2005**, giving 302 one-step-ahead forecasts (the March 2005 forecast has no actual value to compare). The seasonal naïve model is far more accurate: MAE 0.56 vs. 4.01 bcm and RMSE 0.70 vs. 4.36 bcm. Both metrics agree that SNAIVE wins.

### Diebold–Mariano test (5.2)

```{r}
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume), by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
```

**5.2a.** DM = −31.28 with a p-value below 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶. We reject the null of equal forecast accuracy. The negative statistic means the seasonal naïve model has significantly smaller absolute errors than the trend + seasonal dummies model.

### Rolling window (5.3)

```{r}
gas_cv_fc_roll <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc_roll |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Rolling-window (240 months) TS-CV, 1-step-ahead")
```

**5.3a.** With a rolling window, SNAIVE is unchanged (MAE 0.562, RMSE 0.702) because its forecast only uses the value from 12 months earlier, so the window size doesn't matter. The TSLM's accuracy improves a lot: MAE falls from 4.01 to 2.09 and RMSE from 4.36 to 2.42, though it still loses to SNAIVE. As 4.4b showed, the trend isn't a single straight line. With an expanding window, the TSLM keeps fitting one line through the 1960s boom and the 1980s plateau, so its trend and seasonal estimates are out of date. A 20-year rolling window drops the oldest data, so the line adapts to the more recent slope and the smaller recent seasonal swings.

## Reflection

The residuals from the linear trend + seasonal dummies model were far from white noise. They showed long, persistent waves and an ACF that barely decayed over 24 lags, meaning that this month's error strongly predicts next month's. The model was missing two things: a trend that bends over time instead of a single straight line, and seasonality whose size changes over time instead of fixed dummies. Strong positive autocorrelation in the errors is exactly why the seasonal naïve forecast, which simply carries forward recent information, beat the TSLM so decisively in cross-validation, and why the TSLM improved with a rolling window. A better model would use the recent past of the series directly, for example through lagged values or lagged errors (ARIMA/seasonal ARIMA-type dynamics), or a model whose level, trend and seasonal components update over time, like exponential smoothing.
